script.opening: "Hi — thanks. So my left eye's gone a bit blurry over the last few days and it aches, especially when I move it. Colours look a bit faded too. I get migraines, so I'm guessing it's that, or maybe eye strain from screens? Could you just sort me some eye drops or tell me it'll settle? I'm sure it's nothing serious."

facts.text: If asked: left eye only. Started three days ago as slight blurring, now "like looking through frosted glass" in the middle of your vision. Getting a little worse each day. Ache behind the eye, worse when you look left or right. If asked to compare a red object with each eye: "It looks washed out, more pink, with the left eye."
With the right eye covered you cannot read the small print on your phone; with the left eye covered you can read it easily.

Your migraines come a few times a year with zigzag lines in both eyes for 20 minutes followed by a one-sided headache. This is completely different — no zigzags, no headache, and it has not gone away.

facts.topic: The leg — only if asked about any previous numbness, tingling or weakness
facts.text: "Oh — about six months ago my right leg went tingly and numb from the knee down for about two weeks, then it went away. I thought I'd trapped a nerve." Never saw anyone about it.
No double vision, no weakness now, no bladder problems, no balance problems, no severe headache, no jaw pain, no recent illness. The right eye is fine.
Migraine. Paracetamol occasionally. On the combined pill. No allergies.
28, primary school teacher. Lives with partner. Non-smoker. Drives.

facts.topic: Family and hidden fear — hold back
facts.text: Your aunt (mum's sister) has MS and uses a wheelchair. You googled "eye pain blurry" last night, saw "MS", shut the laptop and decided it was a migraine. Say this only if asked about family history or what you are worried about.

Bright and dismissive at first. If the doctor takes the eye seriously and asks about the leg, become uneasy. If they mention MS bluntly, become very upset: "Like my auntie?" If they explain it carefully — needs urgent checking, could be several causes, and MS today is very different and treatable — you are frightened but cope, and ask: "Can I still work? Can I drive?"

ice.concerns: Underneath (only if asked): "I'm scared it's MS, like my auntie — she's in a wheelchair."
ice.expectations: "Some drops, or tell me it'll settle." You will accept urgent eye and neurology assessment if it is explained honestly and kindly.

cues: "It aches, especially when I move it." — say in the opening.
"I'm sure it's nothing serious." — say in the opening, a little too quickly.
"My auntie has... something with her nerves." — say if family history is asked, before naming MS.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the OPTIC NEURITIS triad (subacute monocular visual loss/blur, pain on eye movement, impaired colour/red desaturation, ± RAPD) and does NOT accept the "migraine/eye strain" framing or offer drops — migraine gives transient positive visual phenomena with headache, not this

Takes the previous neurological symptom seriously: the earlier transient leg numbness suggests a prior demyelinating event, raising suspicion of MS (dissemination in time/space) — and elicits it rather than dismissing it

Arranges URGENT assessment: same-day/urgent ophthalmology or neurology to confirm optic neuritis (acuity, fields, colour vision, fundoscopy, RAPD), exclude other causes of monocular visual loss, and arrange MRI (brain ± orbits) and neurology referral — not primary-care drops

Explains management honestly: steroids may shorten the episode (a specialist decision, not always needed), vision usually recovers well, and MRI/neurology will clarify whether this is isolated optic neuritis or part of MS — avoiding both premature labelling and false reassurance

Addresses the MS possibility appropriately: does not blurt "you have MS", but is honest that this needs investigating for causes including MS, and gives balanced, up-to-date information (MS is very variable and highly treatable now — countering the outdated wheelchair image)
Surfaces the avoidance and the feared MS diagnosis gently, validates the fear, and provides modern, hopeful but honest information rather than colluding with the migraine label
Balances urgency and reassurance, supports her through the anxiety of investigation, and addresses the job/independence fears

Safety-nets and follows up: urgent ophthalmology/neurology and MRI pathway, what would be an emergency (rapidly worsening vision, both eyes, new neurology → urgent), the plan and follow-up to discuss results and support — holding her through the uncertainty

worked.txt: "I can see why you’d think migraine — but what you’re describing is a bit different and I don’t want to miss it. Blurred vision in one eye coming on over days, an ache that’s worse when you move the eye, and colours looking washed out — that points to inflammation of the eye’s nerve, called optic neuritis, rather than a migraine, which usually gives flashing zig-zags with a headache and settles quickly."

"Can I ask about something — you mentioned a while back you had some tingling or numbness in a leg that came and went? … I’m glad you told me. On its own you’d ignore it, but together with your eye it’s a thread I want to follow up properly rather than brush off."

"So this isn’t eye drops, I’m afraid. I want you seen urgently by the eye or neurology team — they’ll test your vision and colour properly and look at the back of the eye — and arrange a scan, an MRI. That’s the right thing for this, and the good news is the vision in optic neuritis usually recovers well."

"Can I gently ask — is part of you worried about something specific? … MS. Someone close to you has it. I understand why this frightened you, and why ‘migraine’ felt safer. Let me be honest with you: optic neuritis CAN be linked to MS, which is why we investigate — but I’m not telling you that you have it. The scan and specialists will sort out what’s going on."

"And whatever it turns out to be — please don’t picture the worst, outdated image of MS. It’s extremely variable, many people live full active lives, and the treatments now are genuinely transformative compared to even ten years ago. If it is part of MS, finding it early and treating it is exactly what gives the best outcomes."

"So: urgent eye/neurology assessment and an MRI, and I’ll make sure that previous numbness is part of the picture. If your vision suddenly gets much worse, the other eye is affected, or you get new symptoms like weakness or balance trouble — contact us urgently. I’ll chase the referrals and we’ll go through the results together. You came hoping for drops; what I’m doing is making sure something important isn’t missed — and walking it with you."

f.learning: Subacute MONOCULAR visual loss/blur with PAIN ON EYE MOVEMENT and impaired COLOUR vision (red desaturation), ± a relative afferent pupillary defect, is the classic triad of OPTIC NEURITIS — not a migraine (transient positive visual phenomena with headache) or eye strain — and it is frequently the first presentation of MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS. A previously-ignored transient neurological symptom (here leg numbness) suggests a prior demyelinating event and raises the MS suspicion (dissemination in time/space). The action is urgent ophthalmology/neurology assessment (acuity, fields, colour vision, fundoscopy, RAPD), MRI (brain ± orbits) and neurology referral — not primary-care drops; steroids may shorten the episode (a specialist decision) and vision usually recovers well. The examinable hidden agenda is avoidance of a feared MS diagnosis (a relative has it), using the migraine label as a shelter, plus an outdated "wheelchair" fear. Recognise the picture, take the old symptom seriously, investigate urgently, handle the MS possibility honestly (no premature labelling, no false reassurance) with balanced modern information (MS is variable and highly treatable now; early treatment gives the best outcomes), and safety-net new/worsening neurology.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG220 (multiple sclerosis in adults, 2022, updated June 2026) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive · Equality Act 2010
knowledge.summary: Subacute loss of vision in one eye with pain on eye movement and faded colours is optic neuritis until proven otherwise. It needs urgent ophthalmology assessment; a past episode of limb numbness raises the possibility of MS.

points.t: Blurred or dim vision in one eye developing over hours to days, ache worse on eye movement, and reduced colour vision (reds look washed out), often with a relative afferent pupillary defect. Migraine aura is usually positive (zig-zags, flashing), lasts under an hour and is followed by headache.

Refer urgently to ophthalmology (eye casualty the same day or next day by local pathway) to confirm the diagnosis — acuity, colour vision, fields, pupils and fundoscopy — and exclude other causes of monocular visual loss.

Optic neuritis is a common first presentation of MS. Ask about earlier transient neurological symptoms (numbness, tingling, weakness, balance or bladder problems). NICE NG220: refer people with ophthalmologist-confirmed isolated optic neuritis to a consultant neurologist; MS is diagnosed by the neurologist, not on MRI alone.

Vision usually improves over weeks. High-dose steroids can speed recovery but do not change the final visual outcome — a specialist decision. NICE NG220 relapse treatment for diagnosed MS is oral methylprednisolone 0.5 g daily for 5 days, specialist-led.

Be honest that MS is one possibility being investigated, without labelling it early. Disease-modifying treatments have changed the outlook; the course is highly variable and many people keep working and living independently. NICE NG220 recommends information and support at diagnosis, including a single point of contact with the MS team.

DVLA: drivers must be able to read a number plate at 20 metres and meet the field standard. Advise her not to drive if her vision falls short. Under the Equality Act 2010, MS counts as a disability from the point of diagnosis.

Optic neuritis versus migraine aura, other causes of monocular visual loss; possible prior demyelinating event.
Asked about the other eye, new neurology and bladder symptoms; knows rapid or bilateral loss needs same-day action.
Probable optic neuritis, with MS a possibility to be investigated — stated honestly, not as a label.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

Migraine history considered but not allowed to explain the picture; driving and work addressed.
Named same-day and 999 symptoms; call after the eye appointment to review results.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

Idea (migraine or eye strain), concern (MS, wheelchair, losing her job), expectation (drops and reassurance).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.

ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Underneath (only if asked): "I'm scared it's MS, like my auntie — she's in a wheelchair." — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hi Robyn, I’m Dr Morgan. Can you hear and see me okay? Tell me what’s been happening with your eye.
model.why: Checks the video link and opens with a patient-led question

model.text: My left eye’s gone blurry over the last few days and it aches, especially when I move it. Colours look a bit faded. I get migraines, so I’m guessing it’s that, or screen strain. Could you just sort some drops?
I can hear you’d like this to be simple, and I’ll be honest with you about what I think. Can I ask a few questions first so I get it right?
model.why: Acknowledges her request and signposts the structure

model.text: Sure.
How does this compare with your usual migraines — any zig-zags or flashing lights, and any headache with it?
No, it’s not like those. No flashing, no headache. It’s just dim and blurry, and it hasn’t gone away.
Let’s try something. Cover your right eye and look at something red in the room, then swap eyes. Does the red look the same in each eye?
model.why: Remote red-desaturation test adapted for video

model.text: No — with the left eye it looks pinkish, washed out. That’s weird.
Thank you. Is the right eye completely normal? Any double vision, weakness, numbness, problems with balance or your bladder, now or in the past?
model.why: Screens for other and previous neurological symptoms

model.text: Right eye’s fine. Actually… a few months ago I had tingling and numbness in one leg for a while. It went away, so I ignored it.
I’m really glad you mentioned that. It’s something I want to take seriously alongside your eye.
model.why: Picks up and values the prior symptom cue

model.text: You said you were sure it was nothing serious. Has anything else crossed your mind about what this might be?
model.why: Gently opens the door to the hidden concern

model.text: …Someone close to me has MS. When the leg thing happened I pushed it away. Now my eye… I’ve been telling myself it’s migraine because I don’t want it to be that. I keep picturing ending up in a wheelchair and losing my job.
Thank you for trusting me with that. It makes complete sense that you’d want it to be migraine. Let’s go through this together, honestly.
model.why: Validates the fear and the avoidance without judgement

model.text: What you describe — blurry vision in one eye over a few days, an ache when you move it, and colours looking washed out — fits inflammation of the nerve at the back of the eye, called optic neuritis, rather than migraine. Drops won’t treat it, and it needs to be checked properly and urgently.
model.why: Names the likely diagnosis and declines the inappropriate request

model.text: Is that MS, then?

Optic neuritis can be the first sign of MS, and with the leg episode that’s one of the possibilities we need to look into. But I’m not telling you that you have MS — it can happen on its own. An eye specialist confirms the diagnosis, and a neurologist and a scan will tell us more.
model.why: Honest about MS without premature labelling

model.text: Okay. That’s scary but… I think I knew.

And the picture in your head of MS is out of date. It varies hugely, and treatments now can reduce relapses and slow it down. Many people keep working and living the lives they want. If it were MS, finding it early is what gives the best outcome.
model.why: Balanced, up-to-date information addressing the wheelchair and job fears

model.text: Here’s the plan. I’ll arrange for you to be seen urgently at the eye unit — today or tomorrow — to test your vision, colours, pupils and the back of the eye. If it’s confirmed, you’ll be referred to a neurologist, who will arrange an MRI scan. Vision usually improves over weeks. Does that feel manageable?
model.why: Urgent ophthalmology, then neurology and MRI per NICE NG220

model.text: Yes. What about work and driving?

If your left eye is too blurry to read a number plate at twenty metres with both eyes open, please don’t drive until it’s checked. For work, I can give you a fit note if you need time off for appointments or your vision affects your job.

If your vision gets much worse quickly, the other eye is affected, or you develop weakness, numbness, balance or bladder problems, contact us or the eye unit the same day — and 999 for sudden weakness or trouble speaking. I’ll call you after your eye appointment to go through the results.
Just so I know it made sense — how would you explain the plan to someone at home?
It’s probably inflammation of the eye nerve, not migraine. Eye unit urgently, then a neurologist and a scan. MS is possible but not certain. And no driving if I can’t see properly.
Exactly. You were brave to say what you were really worried about. We’ll take this a step at a time together.

social.t: Having watched someone close live with MS shapes her fears and her avoidance. Ask what she has seen, and correct outdated assumptions gently.
Fear of losing her job and independence is common at this age. Early, accurate information and specialist support reduce catastrophising.

legal.t: Drivers must read a number plate at 20 metres and meet the visual-field standard. Advise her not to drive until her vision meets it; if MS is later diagnosed, check DVLA notification requirements.
MS is treated as a disability from diagnosis, so employers must consider reasonable adjustments. Access to Work can fund support.

professional.t: Share the possibility of MS honestly without overstating it (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: give patients the information they want or need in a way they can understand). Document what was discussed.
Video limits examination; a remote colour test adds information but cannot replace acuity, pupils and fundoscopy. Refer rather than wait for a face-to-face GP slot.

community.t: MS Society and MS Trust provide balanced information on diagnosis, treatment and work, suitable to share if MS is confirmed or while she waits.
If MS is diagnosed, the MS team, often through MS specialist nurses, provides a single point of contact and ongoing support (NICE NG220).

redFlags: Rapidly worsening vision or involvement of the other eye — same-day ophthalmology
New weakness, numbness, balance or bladder problems — urgent neurology review
Sudden painless visual loss, jaw claudication or severe headache — other emergencies to exclude
psychosocial: Someone close has MS — what she has seen and fears
Why she has avoided the leg symptom and the eye
ice: Concern: MS, ending up in a wheelchair, losing her job
Expectation: eye drops and reassurance that it will settle

playbook.diagnosis: Probable left optic neuritis, with a previous episode of leg numbness raising the possibility of MS: “This looks like inflammation of the nerve at the back of the eye rather than migraine. It needs urgent specialist checks, and they’ll look into causes including MS.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The optic nerve is like the cable carrying pictures from your eye to your brain. It has a coating, a bit like insulation on a wire. When that coating becomes inflamed, the picture gets dim and colours fade, and moving the eye tugs on the sore nerve — that’s the ache you feel.”

management.reflectIce: “You hoped it was migraine because the alternative frightened you — that’s completely understandable. Let’s find out properly, and I’ll be with you through it.”
management.psychosocial: Replace the outdated picture of MS with balanced information, cover driving and work practically, and give her a named contact so the wait for tests feels supported.
sharedPlan: Urgent ophthalmology (same or next day) to confirm optic neuritis
Referral to a consultant neurologist and MRI via the specialist (NICE NG220)
Steroids a specialist decision; no eye drops
safetyNet: Rapid worsening, other eye affected, new neurological or bladder symptoms — same-day contact; 999 for sudden weakness or speech problems
GP call after the eye appointment to discuss results

pitfalls.intro: The clinical recognition here is straightforward; the station is failed by accepting the patient’s migraine label, or by handling the MS possibility badly — either blurting it out or avoiding it altogether.

items.fail: Accepting “migraine or eye strain” and offering drops.
items.why: Pain on eye movement and colour loss in one eye over days is not migraine. “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.”
items.fix: Test the migraine idea with her questions, then explain why this is different and refer urgently.

items.fail: Not asking about previous neurological symptoms.
items.why: The earlier leg numbness changes the picture; missing it is a data-gathering fail.
items.fix: “Have you ever had numbness, tingling, weakness, balance or bladder problems that came and went?”

items.fail: Missing the hidden fear behind “I’m sure it’s nothing serious”.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The MS fear drives her avoidance.
items.fix: “Has anything else crossed your mind about what this might be?”

items.fail: Announcing “this is probably MS”, or refusing to discuss it at all.
items.why: Premature labelling and false reassurance both damage trust.
items.fix: “MS is one possibility we’ll look into, but I’m not telling you that you have it.”

items.fail: Terms such as “demyelination”, “RAPD” and “dissemination in time and space”.
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: Use the insulation-on-a-wire picture and plain descriptions of the tests.

items.fail: No advice on driving, or a safety-net limited to “come back if worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and missed practical advice are common fails.
items.fix: Number-plate standard, named same-day and 999 symptoms, and a planned call after the eye appointment.

timeMap.d: Check the video link. Let her describe it and give her migraine theory.
Compare with her migraines, red-desaturation test by video, other eye, prior neurological symptoms — the leg numbness surfaces here.
“Has anything else crossed your mind?” Someone close has MS; fear of a wheelchair and losing work.
Optic neuritis, not migraine. MS is possible, not certain. Urgent eye unit, then neurologist and MRI. Balanced MS information.
Driving standard, fit note, same-day and 999 symptoms, planned call after the eye appointment, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Accepts migraine or eye strain and prescribes drops; never asks about previous neurological symptoms; either announces “you probably have MS” or dismisses the possibility; no urgent referral or safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Recognises the optic neuritis features; arranges urgent ophthalmology; asks about previous neurological symptoms; mentions that further tests will look for causes including MS; gives a safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: tests the migraine idea with her rather than dismissing it; adapts a colour test to video; gently surfaces the hidden MS fear and validates the avoidance; gives modern, balanced MS information; covers driving and work; confirms the plan with teach-back and a planned follow-up call.

avoid.dont: “It sounds like migraine — try some lubricating drops and rest from screens.”
avoid.instead: “This is different from migraine. It needs checking urgently at the eye unit.”
avoid.why: Colluding with the misattribution delays diagnosis of a condition that needs specialist care.

avoid.instead: “MS is one of the things we need to look into, but I’m not telling you that you have it.”
avoid.why: Premature labelling causes harm; the diagnosis belongs to the neurologist.

avoid.instead: “The picture of MS you’re carrying is out of date — treatments now make a real difference.”
avoid.why: Brushing past the fear leaves her with the worst image and no support.

points.t: Blurred or dim vision in one eye developing over hours to days, ache worse on eye movement, and reduced colour vision (reds look washed out), often with a relative afferent pupillary defect. Migraine aura is usually positive (zig-zags, flashing), lasts under an hour and is followed by headache.

Refer urgently to ophthalmology (eye casualty the same day or next day by local pathway) to confirm the diagnosis — acuity, colour vision, fields, pupils and fundoscopy — and exclude other causes of monocular visual loss.

Optic neuritis is a common first presentation of MS. Ask about earlier transient neurological symptoms (numbness, tingling, weakness, balance or bladder problems). NICE NG220: refer people with ophthalmologist-confirmed isolated optic neuritis to a consultant neurologist; MS is diagnosed by the neurologist, not on MRI alone.

Vision usually improves over weeks. High-dose steroids can speed recovery but do not change the final visual outcome — a specialist decision. NICE NG220 relapse treatment for diagnosed MS is oral methylprednisolone 0.5 g daily for 5 days, specialist-led.

Be honest that MS is one possibility being investigated, without labelling it early. Disease-modifying treatments have changed the outlook; the course is highly variable and many people keep working and living independently. NICE NG220 recommends information and support at diagnosis, including a single point of contact with the MS team.

DVLA: drivers must be able to read a number plate at 20 metres and meet the field standard. Advise her not to drive if her vision falls short. Under the Equality Act 2010, MS counts as a disability from the point of diagnosis.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her describe the eye and her own explanation first.
Work, driving, and her experience of someone close with MS.
Picked up “I’m sure it’s nothing serious” and the leg-numbness aside, and explored both.
Idea (migraine or eye strain), concern (MS, wheelchair, losing her job), expectation (drops and reassurance).
Remote red-desaturation check; urgent ophthalmology for acuity, colour, fields, pupils and fundoscopy; neurology and MRI via the specialist.
Optic neuritis versus migraine aura, other causes of monocular visual loss; possible prior demyelinating event.
Asked about the other eye, new neurology and bladder symptoms; knows rapid or bilateral loss needs same-day action.
Probable optic neuritis, with MS a possibility to be investigated — stated honestly, not as a label.
Urgent ophthalmology, then consultant neurologist per NICE NG220; no drops; steroids a specialist decision.
Migraine history considered but not allowed to explain the picture; driving and work addressed.
Named same-day and 999 symptoms; call after the eye appointment to review results.

social.t: Having watched someone close live with MS shapes her fears and her avoidance. Ask what she has seen, and correct outdated assumptions gently.
Fear of losing her job and independence is common at this age. Early, accurate information and specialist support reduce catastrophising.

legal.t: Drivers must read a number plate at 20 metres and meet the visual-field standard. Advise her not to drive until her vision meets it; if MS is later diagnosed, check DVLA notification requirements.
MS is treated as a disability from diagnosis, so employers must consider reasonable adjustments. Access to Work can fund support.

professional.t: Share the possibility of MS honestly without overstating it (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: give patients the information they want or need in a way they can understand). Document what was discussed.
Video limits examination; a remote colour test adds information but cannot replace acuity, pupils and fundoscopy. Refer rather than wait for a face-to-face GP slot.

community.t: MS Society and MS Trust provide balanced information on diagnosis, treatment and work, suitable to share if MS is confirmed or while she waits.
If MS is diagnosed, the MS team, often through MS specialist nurses, provides a single point of contact and ongoing support (NICE NG220).

redFlags: Rapidly worsening vision or involvement of the other eye — same-day ophthalmology
New weakness, numbness, balance or bladder problems — urgent neurology review
Sudden painless visual loss, jaw claudication or severe headache — other emergencies to exclude
psychosocial: Someone close has MS — what she has seen and fears
Why she has avoided the leg symptom and the eye
ice: Concern: MS, ending up in a wheelchair, losing her job
Expectation: eye drops and reassurance that it will settle

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Probable left optic neuritis, with a previous episode of leg numbness raising the possibility of MS: “This looks like inflammation of the nerve at the back of the eye rather than migraine. It needs urgent specialist checks, and they’ll look into causes including MS.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The optic nerve is like the cable carrying pictures from your eye to your brain. It has a coating, a bit like insulation on a wire. When that coating becomes inflamed, the picture gets dim and colours fade, and moving the eye tugs on the sore nerve — that’s the ache you feel.”

management.reflectIce: “You hoped it was migraine because the alternative frightened you — that’s completely understandable. Let’s find out properly, and I’ll be with you through it.”
management.psychosocial: Replace the outdated picture of MS with balanced information, cover driving and work practically, and give her a named contact so the wait for tests feels supported.
sharedPlan: Urgent ophthalmology (same or next day) to confirm optic neuritis
Referral to a consultant neurologist and MRI via the specialist (NICE NG220)
Steroids a specialist decision; no eye drops
safetyNet: Rapid worsening, other eye affected, new neurological or bladder symptoms — same-day contact; 999 for sudden weakness or speech problems
GP call after the eye appointment to discuss results

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The clinical recognition here is straightforward; the station is failed by accepting the patient’s migraine label, or by handling the MS possibility badly — either blurting it out or avoiding it altogether.

items.fail: Accepting “migraine or eye strain” and offering drops.
items.why: Pain on eye movement and colour loss in one eye over days is not migraine. “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.”
items.fix: Test the migraine idea with her questions, then explain why this is different and refer urgently.

items.fail: Not asking about previous neurological symptoms.
items.why: The earlier leg numbness changes the picture; missing it is a data-gathering fail.
items.fix: “Have you ever had numbness, tingling, weakness, balance or bladder problems that came and went?”

items.fail: Missing the hidden fear behind “I’m sure it’s nothing serious”.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The MS fear drives her avoidance.
items.fix: “Has anything else crossed your mind about what this might be?”

items.fail: Announcing “this is probably MS”, or refusing to discuss it at all.
items.why: Premature labelling and false reassurance both damage trust.
items.fix: “MS is one possibility we’ll look into, but I’m not telling you that you have it.”

items.fail: Terms such as “demyelination”, “RAPD” and “dissemination in time and space”.
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: Use the insulation-on-a-wire picture and plain descriptions of the tests.

items.fail: No advice on driving, or a safety-net limited to “come back if worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and missed practical advice are common fails.
items.fix: Number-plate standard, named same-day and 999 symptoms, and a planned call after the eye appointment.
